title: NYC Last-Mile Logistics Gap Analysis
text:
Last-mile delivery — the final leg of a shipment from a distribution facility to the end consumer — is the most expensive and operationally complex segment of any urban supply chain. In a city like New York, where traffic density, limited loading zones, and building access constraints compound the challenge, the proximity of warehouse infrastructure to residential population is a critical determinant of delivery cost and service reliability.
This analysis asks a straightforward question: which NYC neighborhoods lack adequate warehouse coverage, and how many people live in those gaps?
To answer it, I combine 2020 Census population data at the census tract level with NYC’s own property tax lot database (PLUTO) to map industrial and warehouse facilities across the five boroughs. I then apply a 1-mile service radius — a conservative threshold chosen to reflect realistic urban delivery reach given NYC traffic and parking constraints — and identify tracts that fall entirely outside that coverage zone.
The 1-mile threshold is intentionally conservative. A 5-mile radius, standard in suburban logistics models, eliminates virtually all gaps in NYC due to the city’s industrial density. The tighter radius surfaces meaningful variation and reflects the operational reality that a warehouse 4 miles away in Manhattan traffic may be effectively unreachable for same-day delivery.

Data note (updated October 7, 2026): An earlier version of this report (published October 4) showed 38 gap tracts and 169,223 residents, with 14 Manhattan gap tracts. Those numbers were wrong. The Socrata API returns results in pages, and the initial pull hit the default 1,000-row limit, returning an incomplete warehouse dataset. A corrected pull (no row limit) retrieved the full PLUTO industrial lot set. With complete data, Manhattan has near-complete industrial coverage (only 1 gap tract), and the city-wide gap falls to 31 tracts and 61,426 residents. All numbers in this version reflect the corrected pull.

A note on the warehouse data: PLUTO classifies every NYC tax lot by land use code. This analysis filters for code 06 (Industrial & Manufacturing), which includes warehouses, distribution centers, and freight terminals. This is a broader category than warehouses alone — some lots may be light manufacturing or workshops. It represents the best publicly available proxy for logistics infrastructure without purchasing commercial real estate data.

title: NYC Last-Mile Logistics Gap Analysis
text:
Methodology
The analysis follows four steps:
1. Data acquisition. Census tract population and geometry are pulled from the 2020 Decennial Census via the tidycensus package. Borough boundaries come from the Census TIGER/Line files via tigris. Industrial lot locations are queried from the NYC PLUTO dataset via the Socrata JSON API with no row limit, then converted to point geometry using the lot centroid coordinates. Median household income is pulled from the 2020 ACS 5-year estimates.
2. Coordinate reference system. All layers are projected to EPSG:2263 (New York State Plane, Long Island), which uses feet as its unit of measurement. This CRS is optimized for accuracy in the New York metro area and is the standard used by NYC government GIS data.
3. Buffer analysis. Each industrial lot centroid is buffered by 5,280 feet (1 mile). The resulting circles are dissolved into a single merged coverage polygon using st_union(). This merged polygon represents the total area of NYC within 1 mile of at least one industrial facility.
4. Gap identification. Each census tract is tested for intersection with the coverage polygon using st_intersects(). Tracts with no intersection are classified as “far from industrial land.” In addition, the straight-line distance from each tract centroid to its nearest industrial lot is computed using st_distance(), enabling continuous distance-band analysis beyond the binary classification.

title: NYC Last-Mile Logistics Gap Analysis
text:
Results


Code
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)
library(here)
library(knitr)
library(tidyr)

nyc_tracts       <- readRDS(here("data/processed/nyc_tracts_analyzed.rds"))
borough_summary  <- readRDS(here("data/processed/borough_summary.rds"))
warehouses       <- readRDS(here("data/processed/warehouses.rds"))
warehouse_buffer <- readRDS(here("data/processed/warehouse_buffer.rds"))



City-Wide Summary


Code
total_tracts       <- nrow(nyc_tracts)
underserved_tracts <- sum(!nyc_tracts$served)
underserved_pop    <- sum(nyc_tracts$population[!nyc_tracts$served], na.rm = TRUE)
total_pop          <- sum(nyc_tracts$population, na.rm = TRUE)
pct_underserved    <- underserved_pop / total_pop

cat(
  "Total census tracts:             ", comma(total_tracts), "\n",
  "Tracts far from industrial land: ", comma(underserved_tracts), "\n",
  "Population in those tracts:      ", comma(underserved_pop), "\n",
  "Share of total population:       ", percent(pct_underserved, accuracy = 0.1), "\n"
)


Total census tracts:              2,327 
 Tracts far from industrial land:  31 
 Population in those tracts:       61,426 
 Share of total population:        0.7% 


Across NYC’s 2,327 census tracts, 31 tracts containing 61,426 residents fall outside a 1-mile radius of any industrial or warehouse facility. That represents 0.7% of the city’s total population.


Distance-Band Analysis
The binary gap classification (served vs. not) masks variation in how far residents actually are from industrial land. This section reports the share of population within each distance band, by borough, and the median straight-line distance from tract centroid to the nearest industrial lot.
Two distance measures are in use here and they give different numbers intentionally. The borough table (below) classifies a tract as “served” if any part of it intersects a 1-mile buffer – the most generous possible reading. The distance table here uses the tract centroid, which is stricter: a large tract whose center sits 1.1 miles away counts as a gap by centroid even if its edge is technically within range. The 0.7% city-wide figure comes from the buffer method; the centroid method shows about 6% of Queens residents and 12% of Staten Island residents more than a mile from industrial land.


Code
# Requires dist_to_nearest_miles column added by 02_spatial_analysis.R
bands <- c(0.5, 1, 2, 3)

tracts_with_borough <- nyc_tracts |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  mutate(
    borough = case_when(
      substr(GEOID, 3, 5) == "061" ~ "Manhattan",
      substr(GEOID, 3, 5) == "047" ~ "Brooklyn",
      substr(GEOID, 3, 5) == "081" ~ "Queens",
      substr(GEOID, 3, 5) == "005" ~ "Bronx",
      substr(GEOID, 3, 5) == "085" ~ "Staten Island",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(population), !is.na(dist_to_nearest_miles), !is.na(borough))

borough_bands <- tracts_with_borough |>
  group_by(borough) |>
  summarise(
    within_0.5mi   = percent(sum(population[dist_to_nearest_miles <= 0.5]) / sum(population), accuracy = 0.1),
    within_1mi     = percent(sum(population[dist_to_nearest_miles <= 1.0]) / sum(population), accuracy = 0.1),
    within_2mi     = percent(sum(population[dist_to_nearest_miles <= 2.0]) / sum(population), accuracy = 0.1),
    within_3mi     = percent(sum(population[dist_to_nearest_miles <= 3.0]) / sum(population), accuracy = 0.1),
    median_dist_mi = round(median(dist_to_nearest_miles, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(median_dist_mi))

# City-wide row
citywide_band <- tracts_with_borough |>
  summarise(
    borough        = "NYC (all)",
    within_0.5mi   = percent(sum(population[dist_to_nearest_miles <= 0.5]) / sum(population), accuracy = 0.1),
    within_1mi     = percent(sum(population[dist_to_nearest_miles <= 1.0]) / sum(population), accuracy = 0.1),
    within_2mi     = percent(sum(population[dist_to_nearest_miles <= 2.0]) / sum(population), accuracy = 0.1),
    within_3mi     = percent(sum(population[dist_to_nearest_miles <= 3.0]) / sum(population), accuracy = 0.1),
    median_dist_mi = round(median(dist_to_nearest_miles, na.rm = TRUE), 2)
  )

band_table <- bind_rows(borough_bands, citywide_band)

kable(
  band_table |>
    select(
      Borough                    = borough,
      `Within 0.5mi`             = within_0.5mi,
      `Within 1mi`               = within_1mi,
      `Within 2mi`               = within_2mi,
      `Within 3mi`               = within_3mi,
      `Median tract dist. (mi)`  = median_dist_mi

  caption = "Population share within each distance band, by borough (straight-line distance from tract centroid to nearest industrial lot)"

Income Analysis: Does Wealth Drive the Pattern?
The gap tracts are concentrated in outer Queens and Brooklyn — neighborhoods like Bayside, Douglaston, and Marine Park. That raises an obvious question: are these wealthier areas driving warehouses out, or is something else going on? To test this, I pull 2020 ACS median household income by tract and compare the income distributions of gap tracts versus served tracts.


Code
# Load pre-pulled income data (pulled in 01_data_pull.R)
# Avoids calling the Census API at render time.
income_data <- readRDS(here("data/processed/nyc_income.rds"))

nyc_tracts_income <- nyc_tracts |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  left_join(income_data, by = "GEOID") |>
  filter(!is.na(median_income))




Code
income_summary <- nyc_tracts_income |>
  group_by(served) |>
  summarise(
    tracts        = n(),
    median_income = median(median_income, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(group = ifelse(served, "Within 1 mile of industrial land", "Outside 1 mile (gap)"))

kable(
  income_summary |> select(group, tracts, median_income),
  col.names   = c("Group", "Tracts", "Median Household Income"),
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  caption     = "Median household income: gap tracts vs. served tracts (2020 ACS 5-year)"
)

Code
all_gap_median <- median(
  nyc_tracts_income$median_income[!nyc_tracts_income$served], na.rm = TRUE
)
served_median <- median(
  nyc_tracts_income$median_income[nyc_tracts_income$served], na.rm = TRUE
)

cat(
  "Median income, gap tracts (all NYC):  $", comma(round(all_gap_median)), "\n",
  "Median income, served tracts:         $", comma(round(served_median)), "\n",
  "Gap tracts with income data:          ",
  sum(!nyc_tracts_income$served), "of", sum(!nyc_tracts$served), "\n"
)


Median income, gap tracts (all NYC):  $ 101,461 
 Median income, served tracts:         $ 69,275 
 Gap tracts with income data:           17 of 31 


Gap tracts skew higher-income than served tracts ($101,461 vs. $69,275 median household income). That result holds but needs context: only 17 of the 31 gap tracts matched to income data, and Queens — not Manhattan — accounts for most of the gap population (32,622 residents across 13 tracts). Queens gap tracts include outer neighborhoods like Bayside and Douglaston that are solidly middle-to-upper-middle income and genuinely distant from industrial land.
The wealth signal is real but the mechanism is geographic, not political. These are low-density residential neighborhoods at the city’s edge, far from industrial corridors, not wealthy enclaves that pushed industry out. The gap follows the outer edges of the city’s industrial footprint, and those edges happen to overlap with more affluent outer-borough neighborhoods.

title: NYC Last-Mile Logistics Gap Analysis
text:
Discussion

Key Findings
Queens accounts for the largest share of population in the coverage gap (32,622 residents across 13 tracts), followed by Brooklyn (19,809 across 11 tracts). The gap tracts in both boroughs sit at the city’s outer edges — neighborhoods like Bayside, Douglaston, and Marine Park that are far from the industrial corridors concentrated along the waterfront and freight routes closer to the urban core.
Manhattan has only one gap tract (GEOID 36061000100, Census Tract 1 – the Battery Park/financial district waterfront), and it contains zero counted residents. Census Tract 1 is a dense commercial area, not a park or uninhabited land, so the zero count is almost certainly a differential privacy artifact from the 2020 Census rather than a true zero population. The borough’s near-complete coverage reflects the density of industrial lots in specific corridors (West Side railyards, Meatpacking District, Hudson Yards area).
The income data shows gap tracts skew higher-income on average, but this reflects Queens outer neighborhoods, not Manhattan. The Manhattan gap tract itself has no usable population count in this dataset.
The distance-band analysis adds resolution to the binary picture: even among “served” tracts, a meaningful share of the population sits close to the 1-mile boundary. The distance distribution varies significantly by borough, with Staten Island and outer Queens showing longer median distances than Manhattan or the Bronx.


Limitations
Land use proxy. PLUTO code 06 captures industrial lots broadly. A more precise analysis would use actual warehouse operating data from a commercial source (CoStar, CBRE) or cross-reference with business license data. Real last-mile operations in Manhattan often run from garages, retail backrooms, and microhubs classified as commercial or parking in PLUTO — meaning the true coverage may be better than this analysis shows.
Edge effect. This analysis counts only NYC-classified lots. Major distribution hubs across the Hudson in New Jersey (roughly 1 mile from west Manhattan) and just outside the city line in Nassau and Westchester are excluded. This inflates apparent gaps in western Manhattan, Staten Island, and eastern Queens. The effect is largest for Staten Island: the borough sits adjacent to major NJ logistics corridors in Elizabeth and Linden, and its distance numbers would look materially different if cross-Hudson lots were included.
The 1-mile cliff. A tract 1.1 miles from a lot is counted as a gap; one at 0.9 miles is not. The distance-band table above partially addresses this by reporting continuous bands, but the binary classification in the maps and borough table still uses the 1-mile threshold.
Proximity is not service. Being within 1 mile of an industrial lot does not mean being well-served. Delivery reach depends on street network connectivity, curb access, building entry, and operating hours — none of which are in this dataset. Straight-line distance is not travel time.
No cost or feasibility. Identifying a gap area does not mean a micro-fulfillment center belongs there. Rent levels, zoning restrictions, and curb access make many gap areas economically impractical regardless of demand.


Supply Chain Implications
As a first-pass screen of where NYC’s industrial land is relative to its population, this analysis is useful. As a recommendation for where to site logistics infrastructure, it needs the additional context above.
The practical next step is converting straight-line distances to road-network travel times, which would replace the proximity proxy with a measure closer to actual service reach. A retailer or 3PL evaluating NYC market entry needs that layer — along with demand data and real operating constraints — before the gap locations in this analysis become actionable.

text:
Reproducibility
All data is pulled from public APIs at runtime. To reproduce this analysis from scratch:
# 1. Install packages and create folder structure
source("setup.R")

# 2. Pull all data from APIs
source("analysis/01_data_pull.R")

# 3. Run spatial analysis (computes served/unserved and dist_to_nearest_miles)
source("analysis/02_spatial_analysis.R")

# 4. Export maps
source("analysis/03_maps.R")

# 5. Render this report
quarto::quarto_render("report/index.qmd")
